name: Off-Highway Motorcycle
description: A motorized two-wheeler with a seat, designed primarily for off-highway use, such as an electric dirt bike. Ridden on private land with the owner's consent or on public land designated for it, displaying a DNR Off-Highway Vehicle Usage Stamp. No limit on power or speed.

restrictions.rule: Designed to travel primarily off the highway on two wheels, with a seat or saddle for the operator (Illinois Vehicle Code §1-153.1)
No limit on motor power or speed (Illinois Vehicle Code §1-153.1)
Titled with the Secretary of State if bought on or after January 1, 1998

Displays an annual Off-Highway Vehicle Usage Stamp from the Department of Natural Resources, except on land the rider or their immediate family solely owns, at commercial riding parks, in sanctioned competitions, or when it carries a valid motor vehicle registration (Recreational Trails of Illinois Act, 20 ILCS 862/26, 862/34)
Needs a separate off-highway vehicle trails public access sticker to ride in public OHV parks funded by the state grant program (Recreational Trails of Illinois Act, 20 ILCS 862/25.5)

Ridden on public land only where it's designated for all-terrain vehicles or off-highway motorcycles, and on private land only with the owner's or lessee's consent; never in nature preserves or on railroad tracks or rights-of-way (Illinois Vehicle Code §11-1427)

Not allowed on streets, highways or roadways unless a local government or the Department of Transportation authorizes it there, and then only where the posted limit is 35 mph or less, by a licensed driver, with the required lights, mirror, brakes and turn signals and liability insurance
Never ridden on or directly across a tollroad, interstate or controlled access highway
No state OHV safety certificate or course is required

One with an electric motor rated above 750 W up to 8,000 W is also a motor driven cycle: bought new, it must be titled if it has a VIN, and it can be registered for the road only if built and equipped for highway use
